title: The Implications of Using Estimated Solar Radiation on the Derivation of Potential Evapotranspiration and Soil Moisture Deficit within an Embankment
abstract: In the absence of measured data, evapotranspiration is commonly estimated at a given site according to the methods outlined by Allen et al. (1998). Their work provides a system of calculation to derive the solar radiation values required to predict the available energy for water vaporisation. As such estimations of evapotranspiration are very dependent on the available data. In this work, meteorological parameters including air temperature, relative humidity, wind speed, near-surface soil temperature, shortwave and net solar radiation were measured for a complete year at the BIONICS trial embankment, Newcastle, UK. Estimates were made of the net radiation for a number of cases (1. no radiation data and 2. measured incident short wave radiation) and compared to the field monitored values. These data were in turn used to estimate the potential evapotranspiration (ETp) from the embankment. The results indicate that the net radiation and hence ETp derived entirely from estimated data are significantly higher than those derived with measured shortwave or net radiation. Results for estimates of ETp derived from monitored shortwave and net radiation data are a close match to each other. In order to investigate the potential effects on slope stability, an assessment of soil moisture deficit was undertaken. The results indicate that numerical models using the varying estimates of ETp would likely produce different results in terms of generated suctions and suction dissipation and so undergo different magnitudes of shrink-swell cycling, in turn leading to varying rates of strain softening behaviour, differing calculated factors of safety and differing modelled time to failure.

## The Implications of Using Estimated Solar Radiation on the Derivation of Potential Evapotranspiration and Soil Moisture Deficit within an Embankment

## Peter Helm[1] , Ross Stirling[1] and Stephanie Glendinning[1]

_1Newcastle University,Newcastle-upon-Tyne, U.K. peter.helm@newcastle.ac.uk, ross.stirling@newcastle.ac.uk_

## **Abstract**

In the absence of measured data, evapotranspiration is commonly estimated at a given site according to the methods outlined by Allen et al. (1998). Their work provides a system of calculation to derive the solar radiation values required to predict the available energy for water vaporisation. As such estimations of evapotranspiration are very dependent on the available data.In this work, meteorological parameters including air temperature, relative humidity, wind speed, near-surface soil temperature, shortwave and net solar radiation were measured for a complete year at the BIONICS trial embankment, Newcastle, UK.

Estimates were made of the net radiation for a number of cases (1. no radiation data and 2. measured incident short wave radiation) and compared to the field monitored values.  These data were in turn used to estimate the potential evapotranspiration () from the embankment. The results indicate that the net radiation and hence  derived entirely from estimated data are significantly higher than those derived with measured shortwave or net radiation. Results for estimates of  derived from  monitored shortwave and net radiation data are a close match to each other.

In order to investigate the potential effects on slope stability, an assessment of soil moisture deficit was undertaken. The results indicate that numerical models using the varying estimates of  would likely produce different results in terms of generated suctions and suction dissipation and so undergo different magnitudes of shrink-swell cycling, in turn leading to varying rates of strain softening behaviour, differing calculated factors of safety and differing modelled time to failure.

_Keywords:_ Evapotranspiration, Net radiation, Soil moisture deficit, Slope stability

## 1 Introduction

A significant factor influencing infrastructure slope stability is the fluctuation of pore water pressures due to changing weather patterns. Researchers have investigated the influence of changing

weather on infrastructure slope pore water pressures (Smethurst et al., 2006; 2012; Glendinning et al., 2014 amongst others) as well as the resultant effect of fluctuating pore pressures on stability via laboratory and numerical modelling studies (Potts et al., 1997; Nyambayo et al., 2004; O’Brien et al, 2004; Ellis and O’Brien, 2007; Rouainia et al, 2009; Nyambayo and Potts, 2010; Take and Bolton, 2011; Davies et al., 2014).

Dijkstra and Dixon (2010) highlighted the extremely wet winter conditions in 2000-2001 which led to widespread slope failures in south east England, Wales and Scotland which is further evidence of the influence of rainfall on stability. However along with the influence of antecedent rainfall in triggering instability,  progressive failure and strength reduction is also a significant mechanism in the behavior of infrastructure slopes, particularly in high plasticity over consolidated clays (see for example Potts et al., 1997; Leroueil, 2001: Take and Bolton, 2011). This mechanism typically requires shrink-swell behavior to occur over time and in turn requires moisture content (and pore water pressure) changes in the soil which at the near surface are generated by rainfall (as previously mentioned) and evapotranspiration ().

The process of evapotranspiration will act to remove water from the near surface and in the zone of influence of vegetation roots, leading to the generation of suctions, elevated effective stress and hence volume change. As such to model shrink-swell behavior and its influence on progressive failure in high plasticity clays it is in turn necessary to derive the near surface water balance.  The rainfall reaching the soil surface can be measured directly, however the evapotranspiration is most commonly estimated from meteorological parameters recorded at or near the site of interest.

Potential evapotranspiration () is commonly estimated using the Penman-Monteith equation (Montieth, 1965) which requires a number of meteorological parameters. The majority of these are measured directly, however the net radiation flux (  ) is commonly estimated from monitored incident shortwave radiation () using the methods outlined by Allen et al. (1998). In the absence of measured shortwave radiation it may in turn be estimated based on a calculation of the extraterrestrial radiation ().

In this work the potential evapotranspiration (  ) occurring from the surface of a trial infrastructure embankment is estimated using the procedures outlined above. In turn the influence of the resultant  on soil moisture deficit (used as a proxy for slope stability) is investigated in order to attempt to provide guidance on the requirements for the monitoring of meteorological parameters as inputs for numerical modelling.

The site used for this work was the BIONICS embankment which was constructed in 2005 and is located at Nafferton Farm near Stocksfield, Northumberland, UK (OS Grid Reference: ). The construction and extensive research activity at this site is described in more detail by Hughes et al. (2009) and Glendinning et al. (2014).

## 2 Potential Evapotranspiration

The two processes of evaporation and transpiration are together commonly referred to as evapotranspiration (). A detailed discussion of these processes is given in Allen et al. (1998). A very brief summary of the most significant details is given here.

The process whereby liquid water is converted to water vapor (vaporisation) and removed from the evaporating surface (vapor removal) is known as evaporation. In order for this to occur energy is required. The source of this energy includes direct solar radiation and (to a lesser extent) the ambient temperature of the air. For this water vapor to be removed, it is necessary for there to be a difference between the vapor pressure at the evaporating surface and the surrounding atmosphere (known as vapor pressure deficit). As the process of evaporation continues the surrounding air becomes saturated and hence the vapor pressure difference decreases, which in turn reduces the evaporation rate. In order to maintain the rate of evaporation it is necessary to replace the saturated air with drier air. This process is strongly dependent on wind speed.  As such evaporation is controlled to a greater or lesser extent by the following meteorological parameters: solar radiation, air temperature, air humidity (which controls vapor pressure and hence vapor pressure deficit) and wind speed.

The vaporisation and loss of water from vegetation to the atmosphere is known as transpiration. This loss primarily occurs from small openings in plant leaves known as stomata.  Water is taken up by the plant roots, transported through the plant and the vast majority is in turn lost to atmosphere. Transpiration, along with evaporation, depends on the supply of energy, the vapor pressure gradient and wind. As such the same meteorological parameters described previously for evaporation are important. However unlike in the evaporation process, plant physiology also plays a role in transpiration.

Where the supply of water to the evaporating surface is sufficient to meet the evaporative demand, the only limits on the evaporation rate are the meteorological conditions and evaporation is occurring at a maximum rate, known as the potential rate (). However in situations where the recharge of water to the evaporating surface is limited, the water content of the soil at the near surface will drop. This in turn will decrease the effective permeability of the near surface soil and act to limit evaporation. Further to this, any changes in soil water content and hence unsaturated permeability will also effect the transpiration rate as will the type of vegetation. These factors will all act to limit the rate of evapotranspiration to a level below thepotential rate. This limited rate is described as the actual evapotranspiration rate ().

## 5 Discussion and Conclusions

## 5.1 Implications for Slope Stability

As described in section 4.3, there is an observed correlation between times of low / zero  and slope failure (Ridley et al., 2004). However depending on the method used to derive  and hence  and  the same site could be shown to be either constantly returning to a state of zero  and hence be at greater risk of slope failure, or at the other extreme apparently in a state of continual increased  with the resultant implication of elevated pore suctions and hence high effective stresses and shear strengths which would be indicative of an increased factor of safety of the slope.

Further to this, precipitation and evapotranspiration (or the meteorological parameters required to calculate evapotranspiration) are commonly used as inputs to numerical models used in slope stability analysis (see for example Rouainia et al., 2009; Davies et al., 2014) or for modelling changes in slope pore water pressures (e.g. Briggs et al., 2013). The generation of suctions as suggested by increased  would also be indicative of low unsaturated permeability which would have potential implications for flow in to, out of, and within the slope; further complicating any attempt to model site hydrology over time.

Coupled hydro-mechanical modelling, particularly of the type undertaken to assess the stability of slopes in high plasticity over-consolidated clays commonly found in southern England and which are prone to shrink swell behavior (see for example Potts et al., 1997; Ellis and O’Brien, 2007) would be significantly affected by the assumed level of evapotranspiration and the potential for zero soil moisture deficit as both these factors would influence volume change (shrinkage and swelling respectively) and lead to the development of strain softening behavior within the models. The rate at which this softening occurs would in turn have significant implications for the modelled time to slope failure and the calculated factor of safety of the slope at any given time. As such, the assumptions relating to the choice of meteorological parameters, and how they may influence the results would

## 5.2 Suggestions for Monitoring Solar Radiation

It seems clear from the results presented, that the use of estimated solar radiation from extraterrestrial radiation in the absence of monitored data appears to significantly over estimate the level of net radiation and hence evapotranspiration. To further compound the uncertainty regarding the estimation of  and  from monitored  data, it can also be seen that while the  data monitored on the embankment appears to overestimate the level of  compared to that derived from direct  monitoring, the Nafferton Farm data seems to show the opposite trend.  Unlike the embankment meteorological station, the Nafferton farm weather station is located on flat ground and is at a slightly lower altitude.  The radiation sensor is also of a different type to that used on the embankment. As such it is not possible to say for certain with the data available whether an individual difference or some combination of parameters is responsible for this difference in measured .

Ultimately, it would appear, that the choice of meteorological monitoring equipment as well as the siting of said equipment has the potential to influence the results of modelling undertaken using derived parameters, and as such careful thought should be given to the source data. Where possible, as a minimum, shortwave radiation data should be employed to estimate net radiation and hence  and ideally net radiation sensors should be used where possible in the absence of actual evapotranspiration measurement.
